briefs.bpd:
Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant

neonatal respiratory distress causes · bronchopulmonary dysplasiaHow preterm, did labor occur, when did it start, and what does the film show?

WorkupDistress at birthPreterm clockPractice
Bottom line

Time it first. At birth, four facts decide before any pathophysiology: gestational age, whether labor occurred, when distress began and what the film shows; the oxygen response then separates lung from shunt. In the preterm infant each complication owns a window: check the timing before the findings.

  • Transient tachypnea of the newborn: retained fetal lung fluid in structurally normal term lungs; fluid in the fissures; onset within 2 hours, gone within 24 to 72.
  • Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS): preterm surfactant deficiency; distress at birth, ground glass with air bronchograms.
  • Apnea of prematurity: the immature brainstem does not sustain breathing; central pauses, with no obstruction and no lung disease, in an infant well between episodes.
  • Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD): a preterm infant still on supplemental oxygen at 28 days of life or more; arrested alveolar development, not fibrotic ventilator injury and not air leak.
Workup
Distress at birth
Gestational age, labor, onset, film
DiagnosisSettingThe tell
Transient tachypneaTerm or late preterm; cesarean without labor, macrosomia, maternal diabetes or asthmaFluid in the fissures, perihilar streaking; resolves in 24 to 72 hours
Respiratory distress syndromePreterm surfactant deficiency, worsening over 48 to 72 hoursLow lung volumes, diffuse ground glass with air bronchograms
Meconium aspirationTerm or post-term, meconium-stained fluid, fetal distressCoarse, patchy, asymmetric infiltrates with hyperinflation
Group B streptococcal pneumoniaRupture 18 hours or more, maternal fever, no intrapartum prophylaxisFilm mimics RDS exactly; temperature instability, neutropenia
Congenital diaphragmatic herniaViscera crush the developing lungScaphoid abdomen, shifted heart sounds; bowel loops in the chest with a displaced heart
Persistent pulmonary hypertension Can't missFailed transition, often after asphyxia or aspirationPre- to postductal gap above 10%, poorly oxygen-responsive
PolycythemiaIntrauterine hypoxia or placental transfusionPlethora with hypoglycemia and a clear film; venous hematocrit above 65% in a term neonate
Exit ramps Diaphragmatic hernia – never bag-mask (it inflates bowel inside the chest): intubate, ventilate with limited pressures (the hypoplastic lung is at risk of barotrauma ⚠︎), decompress with a nasogastric tube; the lungs stay small after repair, and the pulmonary hypertension persists · Displaced heart sounds – scaphoid abdomen with absent breath sounds on the defect side: hernia; distended, hyperresonant hemithorax in a deteriorating infant: tension pneumothorax, needle decompression; well, heart on the right, no distress: dextrocardia · Diabetic mother – raises the risk of transient tachypnea and delays surfactant maturation, so RDS can appear at a gestational age that would otherwise be safe
The preterm clock
Apnea of prematurity Definition – a pause over 20 seconds, or a shorter one with bradycardia or desaturation · Diagnosis – clinical, after the mimics are checked: anemia, infection and intraventricular hemorrhage, plus glucose and electrolytes (seizure and reflux are the other usual mimics) · Versus hemorrhage – lethargy, a tense fontanelle, a growing head or seizures; cranial ultrasound · Management – caffeine, a methylxanthine brainstem stimulant; add continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or high-flow nasal cannula if spells continue
Bronchopulmonary dysplasia Severity – graded by support required at 36 weeks postmenstrual age · Prevention – antenatal steroids plus surfactant turned it from fibrotic injury into developmental arrest; caffeine and vitamin A each reduce it · Management – supportive: oxygen, nutrition, fluid restriction; alveoli keep forming over months · Complications – pulmonary hypertension, systemic hypertension, recurrent respiratory infections, neurodevelopmental delay · Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) – first season, under 8 months: nirsevimab or clesrovimab; second season, 8 to 19 months: nirsevimab only, for BPD that needed oxygen, diuretics or chronic corticosteroids in the 6 months before the season; palivizumab is no longer available after December 31, 2025 (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention guidance)
Practice
  1. 1-hour-old boy born at 40 weeks by cesarean without labor is tachypneic chest x-ray shows fluid in the interlobar fissures Afebrile · birth weight 4200 g · respiratory rate 80/min · oxygen saturation 88% on room air, 98% on oxygen → Transient tachypnea of the newborn → retained fetal lung fluid in structurally normal term lungs: fluid in the fissures appears in no competing diagnosis, and saturation correcting from 88% to 98% on oxygen is alveolar fluid, not a shunt. Cesarean without labor misses the catecholamine surge that switches the epithelium to absorbing fluid; macrosomia adds risk. Respiratory distress syndrome is the right category but a preterm member, and group B streptococcal pneumonia needs risk factors the stem never supplies. Supportive care: onset within 2 hours, and it resolves within 24 to 72 hours, so an infant breathing normally by 48 hours fits
  2. 6-week-old boy born at 26 weeks still needs supplemental oxygen on nasal cannula oxygen every day since birth enteral feeds introduced today Weight gain appropriate on total parenteral nutrition Afebrile · oxygen saturation 92% on 0.5 L/min → Arrested alveolar development → a preterm infant still on supplemental oxygen at 28 days or more has bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and since antenatal steroids and surfactant it is arrested alveolar development: fewer alveoli, less septation, disrupted vasculogenesis. Fibrotic ventilator injury is the old form, and air leak belongs to the first days on high pressures, weeks before this. Feeds introduced today suggest refeeding syndrome, but appropriate weight gain on total parenteral nutrition excludes prior malnutrition
  3. 6-hour-old girl born at term has tachypnea and grunting membranes ruptured 24 hours before delivery maternal fever 38.5 °C in labor; no intrapartum prophylaxis Temperature unstable since birth T 35.9 °C · HR 176/min · respiratory rate 74/min → Blood culture and empiric ampicillin plus gentamicin → rupture 18 hours or more, maternal fever and no intrapartum prophylaxis, with temperature instability, is early-onset group B streptococcal sepsis. Its film mimics respiratory distress syndrome exactly, so surfactant misses it, and observing without antibiotics leaves the infection untreated: culture and start ampicillin and gentamicin
  4. 1-day-old girl born at term after delayed cord clamping is plethoric jittery and irritable before feeds Feeding well; no hepatomegaly; normal genitalia Afebrile · venous hematocrit 70% · glucose 35 mg/dL · HR 150/min → Red cells consume glucose → delayed cord clamping adds blood, and the expanded red cell mass takes up glucose, giving hypoglycemia and hypocalcemia; breakdown of the cells adds hyperbilirubinemia. Liver congestion is not the mechanism ⚠︎, and salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia brings ambiguous genitalia in girls, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia, days later
  5. Term newborn boy has severe respiratory distress at delivery scaphoid abdomen heart sounds displaced to the right chest x-ray shows bowel gas in the left hemithorax T 36.6 °C · HR 92/min · oxygen saturation 64% → Intubate with limited peak pressures and decompress the stomach → a scaphoid abdomen with displaced heart sounds and bowel in the chest is a diaphragmatic hernia. Bag-mask ventilation inflates bowel inside the chest, so intubate, ventilate with limited pressures (the hypoplastic lung is at risk of barotrauma ⚠︎) and decompress with a nasogastric tube. Needle decompression is for a tension pneumothorax: a distended, hyperresonant hemithorax in a deteriorating infant
  6. 4-day-old boy born at 29 weeks in neonatal intensive care several 20-second breathing pauses today, bradycardia and desaturation ends with stimulation; pink, active, feeding well between Cultures negative; antibiotics stopped T 36.9 °C, stable · glucose, electrolytes, hemoglobin, ultrasound normal → Begin caffeine → a central pause from an immature brainstem, starting on day 2 to 3 in an infant who is well between spells, with the mimics checked (infection, anemia, intraventricular hemorrhage, glucose, electrolytes), is apnea of prematurity. Caffeine is a methylxanthine brainstem stimulant; add CPAP or high-flow nasal cannula if spells continue. Antibiotics answer the infant who is ill between spells; dexamethasone and albuterol are used for bronchopulmonary dysplasia, not for apnea
  7. 2-hour-old boy born at 29 weeks is grunting and retracting chest x-ray shows low lung volumes diffuse ground-glass opacity with air bronchograms Membranes ruptured at delivery T 36.8 °C · respiratory rate 72/min · oxygen saturation 86% on room air → Respiratory distress syndrome → surfactant deficiency in a preterm infant (under 34 weeks) gives distress at birth, worsening over 48 to 72 hours, with low volumes, ground glass and air bronchograms: give surfactant and CPAP. Transient tachypnea shows fluid in the fissures in a term infant; group B streptococcal pneumonia mimics this film exactly but needs risk factors (rupture 18 hours or more, maternal fever, no intrapartum prophylaxis) this stem does not supply
  8. 2-day-old boy born at term is plethoric, lethargic and feeding poorly venous hematocrit 72% no better after 12 hours of intravenous fluids Born after delayed cord clamping Afebrile · glucose 48 mg/dL · HR 156/min → Partial exchange transfusion → most polycythemic infants are ruddy and asymptomatic; hyperviscosity brings lethargy, irritability and jitteriness, and in severe cases tachypnea, respiratory distress, poor feeding and cyanosis. Hydration by feeds or glucose-containing intravenous fluids comes first; symptomatic hyperviscosity despite it needs a partial exchange transfusion, which swaps blood for saline to lower viscosity. A double-volume exchange swaps blood for blood and leaves the hematocrit high, and furosemide removes plasma water and concentrates the blood ⚠︎; true dehydration is rare in the first 2 days, while the neonate still carries excess extracellular fluid
  9. 8-hour-old boy born at 41 weeks is cyanotic preductal saturation 88%, postductal 76% minimal improvement on 100% oxygen chest x-ray nearly clear Delivered through meconium-stained fluid Afebrile · HR 168/min · BP 62/38 mm Hg → Obtain an echocardiogram → a pre- to postductal gap above 10% that barely responds to oxygen is right-to-left ductal shunting: persistent pulmonary hypertension, a failed transition often after asphyxia or aspiration. Echocardiography shows high pulmonary pressure in a structurally normal heart and excludes cyanotic heart disease. Surfactant treats alveolar disease, which corrects on oxygen, and reassurance misses a can't-miss diagnosis
  10. 12-day-old girl born at 26 weeks has abdominal distension bloody stools on day 10 of enteral feeds abdominal x-ray shows pneumatosis intestinalis T 35.9 °C · HR 182/min · capillary refill 4 seconds → Necrotizing enterocolitis → a preterm infant on enteral feeds with distension, bloody stools and pneumatosis intestinalis has bacterial invasion of the bowel wall: keep nil by mouth, give intravenous antibiotics and consult surgery. Allergic proctocolitis is the well infant with bloody stool; pneumatosis intestinalis is the tell that names this can't-miss diagnosis over it and over malrotation with volvulus
  11. 1-hour-old boy born at 39 weeks by cesarean without labor is breathing fast chest x-ray shows fluid in the fissures with perihilar streaking Mother asks to breastfeed now Afebrile · respiratory rate 80/min · oxygen saturation 93% on oxygen → Keep nil by mouth with intravenous fluids and supplemental oxygen → neonatal tachypnea is a respiratory rate above 60 per minute, and feeding at a rate of 80 risks aspiration: keep nil by mouth with intravenous fluids and oxygen. Intubation and surfactant are for the preterm surfactant-deficient lung, not retained fluid in a term infant
  12. 24-year-old woman, gravida 1, is in preterm labor at 29 weeks cervix dilated 5 cm delivery expected within 48 hours T 37.0 °C · BP 118/72 mm Hg · fetal heart rate 140/min → Antenatal betamethasone → antenatal betamethasone gives the fetal lung the cortisol signal that drives surfactant maturation (the signal fetal hyperinsulinism antagonizes); steroids before delivery, with surfactant after birth, converted bronchopulmonary dysplasia from fibrotic injury to developmental arrest; postnatal surfactant gives up the antenatal dose, and tocolysis only buys time for the steroid course; it does not mature the lung ⚠︎
  13. 1-hour-old boy born at 37 weeks has grunting and retractions mother has poorly controlled diabetes chest x-ray shows diffuse ground glass with air bronchograms Afebrile · birth weight 4300 g · oxygen saturation 85% on room air → Fetal hyperinsulinism antagonises cortisol, delaying surfactant maturation → fetal hyperinsulinism antagonizes cortisol and suppresses phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylglycerol production, delaying surfactant maturation; the pneumocytes are not directly injured, and placental insufficiency is not the mechanism here ⚠︎
  14. 5-day-old girl born at 30 weeks has new apnea and bradycardia since this morning lethargic and mottled between episodes abdominal distension and feeding intolerance No antibiotics so far T 35.8 °C, unstable · HR 188/min · capillary refill 4 seconds → Blood culture and empiric antibiotics → an infant who is ill between spells (temperature instability, feeding intolerance or poor perfusion) has suspected sepsis, not simple apnea of prematurity: culture and treat. Caffeine is for the infant well between spells; anemia of prematurity comes weeks later, pale with a low hemoglobin; this tachycardia is sepsis
  15. 2-day-old girl was diagnosed with a left congenital diaphragmatic hernia at birth intubated; saturations now falling echocardiogram shows suprasystemic pulmonary pressures right hand saturation 92% · foot saturation 78% · HR 170/min → Inhaled nitric oxide → a hand-foot gap above 10% is right-to-left ductal shunting from pulmonary hypertension of the hypoplastic lung. Prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) is the right class for a cyanotic newborn, but this cyanosis is not a closing duct; a chest tube treats a pneumothorax, not shunting. The lungs stay small after repair, and the pulmonary hypertension persists; the gap itself shows the duct is already open, so the target is pulmonary vasodilation
  16. 3-day-old boy born at 27 weeks has abrupt hypoxia on high-pressure mechanical ventilation since birth chest x-ray shows unilateral perivascular cystic lucencies No distended, hyperresonant hemithorax Afebrile · HR 172/min · oxygen saturation 78% → Pulmonary interstitial emphysema → air dissects into the interstitium on high ventilator pressures in the first days: cystic lucencies and abrupt decompensation; reduce ventilator pressures. Tension pneumothorax gives a distended, hyperresonant hemithorax needing needle decompression, and respiratory distress syndrome, though it worsens over 48 to 72 hours, shows ground glass with air bronchograms
  17. 10-hour-old girl born at 29 weeks has needed CPAP since birth rising oxygen requirement, now 60% worsening retractions chest x-ray shows ground glass with air bronchograms T 36.8 °C · oxygen saturation 86% on CPAP → Intubate and give surfactant → worsening surfactant deficiency despite CPAP means CPAP has failed: intubate and give surfactant. Closer observation leaves the failure untreated, and antibiotics alone do not replace surfactant
  18. 6-hour-old boy born at term is ruddy and jittery breathing fast with no retractions chest x-ray is clear; no hepatomegaly; normal heart sounds Mother had preeclampsia Afebrile · glucose 32 mg/dL · respiratory rate 70/min · HR 150/min → Polycythemia → plethora with hypoglycemia and a clear film is polycythemia. Intrauterine hypoxia drives erythropoietin (preeclampsia, maternal diabetes or hypertension, smoking, growth restriction), or placental transfusion adds blood (delayed cord clamping, twin-twin transfusion); hyperviscosity brings jitteriness, and in severe cases tachypnea, and the expanded red cell mass takes up glucose; check a venous hematocrit (above 65%). Transient tachypnea shows fluid in the fissures, glycogen storage disease type I brings hepatomegaly and lactic acidosis, and cyanotic heart disease is excluded by a normal heart and exam
  19. 14-month-old boy born at 30 weeks is seen at a well visit has bronchopulmonary dysplasia, on diuretics until 3 months ago his second RSV season starts next month Afebrile · respiratory rate 36/min · oxygen saturation 96% on room air → Nirsevimab prophylaxis → chronic lung disease of prematurity that needed medical support (supplemental oxygen, diuretics or chronic corticosteroids) in the 6 months before the second season qualifies for a second-season dose, and nirsevimab is the product recommended; palivizumab is no longer available from December 31, 2025, and the prophylaxis is an antibody, not an infant vaccine ⚠︎
  20. Term newborn girl has severe cyanosis at 12 hours no improvement on 100% oxygen no retractions; comfortable tachypnea chest radiograph structurally normal Afebrile · oxygen saturation 68% on 100% oxygen · HR 160/min → Prostaglandin E1 infusion → cyanosis that does not correct on oxygen in a comfortable infant with a normal film is a shunt (the hyperoxia test, still keyed on exams though largely abandoned clinically): suspect cyanotic congenital heart disease and start prostaglandin E1 pending echocardiography. Surfactant treats alveolar disease that corrects on oxygen; inhaled nitric oxide treats pulmonary hypertension, whose tell is a ductal saturation gap above 10%
  21. 3-week-old boy born at 28 weeks is given caffeine for central apneic spells well between spells His parents ask when the spells should stop Afebrile · HR 150/min · oxygen saturation 97% on room air → By about his expected due date → the brainstem breathing center matures by term corrected age, so spells resolve by about the expected due date; 28 days is the bronchopulmonary dysplasia clock, not the apnea clock
  22. 1-hour-old boy born at 41 weeks has tachypnea and retractions delivered through meconium-stained fluid after fetal distress chest x-ray shows coarse, patchy, asymmetric infiltrates with hyperinflation Afebrile · respiratory rate 84/min · oxygen saturation 87% → Meconium aspiration syndrome → term or post-term delivery through meconium-stained fluid after fetal distress, with coarse patchy asymmetric infiltrates and hyperinflation; watch for pneumothorax and pulmonary hypertension. Transient tachypnea shows fluid in the fissures, and for congenital pneumonia nothing in this stem points to infection (rupture 18 hours or more, maternal fever, no intrapartum prophylaxis) ⚠︎
  23. 2-hour-old girl born at 36 weeks has central cyanosis, grunting and retractions mother has poorly controlled type 2 diabetes chest x-ray shows bilateral ground-glass opacities Afebrile · saturation 64% rising to 82% on oxygen · pre- and postductal readings equal → Surfactant → maternal diabetes delays surfactant maturation, so an infant of a diabetic mother can develop respiratory distress syndrome at a gestational age that would otherwise be safe. Ground glass with equal pre- and postductal readings and a partial oxygen response is lung disease, not a ductal shunt, so prostaglandin E1 is not the answer; steroids for the lung are the antenatal betamethasone given before delivery
  24. 4-month-old boy born at 28 weeks has poor weight gain needed supplemental oxygen until 3 months of age loud P2 liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin Afebrile · respiratory rate 56/min · oxygen saturation 93% on room air → Pulmonary artery hypertension → pulmonary hypertension is a complication of bronchopulmonary dysplasia that arrives months later, with a loud P2 and poor growth: obtain an echocardiogram. Systemic hypertension and recurrent respiratory infections are also complications, but a loud P2 is the pulmonic sound, and chronic aspiration does not explain it ⚠︎; the enlarged liver is right heart failure
  25. 4-day-old girl born at term was diagnosed with transient tachypnea on day 1 still breathing fast at 96 hours of life Feeding by nasogastric tube Afebrile · respiratory rate 74/min · oxygen saturation 94% on room air → Re-evaluate for another diagnosis → transient is a diagnostic criterion, not a description: it resolves within 24 to 72 hours, so tachypnea beyond 72 hours means the diagnosis was wrong; look again. Continued observation and discharge both keep the wrong label
Common wrong answers Refeeding syndrome: feeds introduced today suggest it, but appropriate weight gain on total parenteral nutrition excludes prior malnutrition. Pulmonary interstitial emphysema at 28 days: real ventilator pathology, but it belongs to the first days. RDS in a term infant: the right category, a preterm member. Group B streptococcal pneumonia: needs risk factors the stem must supply. Prostaglandin in a diaphragmatic hernia: the right class for a cyanotic newborn, but the cyanosis comes from hypoplastic lungs and pulmonary hypertension, not a closing duct. Diaphragmatic hernia at an hour with fissural fluid: it presents at delivery with a scaphoid abdomen.
Pairs with Part I Stool Changes in a Well Infant: the well infant with bloody stool; here, the ill preterm infant. Ask: is the infant preterm, distended and unwell? Part II Follow-Up of the Preterm Infant: intraventricular hemorrhage and anemia of prematurity, the mimics to exclude before calling a spell apnea of prematurity. Ask: is the infant well between episodes? Part II Posterior Urethral Valves: the same distress in the first hours. Ask: is this fluid in normal lungs, or lungs that never developed? Part I Cyanosis in the Newborn: the step before, where work of breathing, the oxygen response and the limb gradient sort lung from heart. Part I Hypoxemia: the physiology under the oxygen response.
Transferable rule

Match the clock before the findings. Birth: RDS or transient tachypnea, sorted by gestational age, labor, onset and the film. Ventilator days: air leak. Day 2 to 3 spells in a well infant: apnea of prematurity. Oxygen at 28 days: BPD. Months: pulmonary hypertension. When the history states a diagnostic criterion exactly, make that diagnosis directly.
